endorsements.quote: At minimum, high-impact clinical AI systems should undergo subgroup-disaggregated evaluation before deployment, periodic postdeployment reassessment after major updates or material workflow changes, and formal review and remediation planning when subgroup performance falls below prespecified, context-specific clinical acceptability thresholds [ 9 , 18 , 29 , 31 ].

These thresholds should be defined prospectively according to the system’s intended clinical function, risk level, and potential consequences of error and may include minimum subgroup performance levels, calibration requirements, maximum allowable subgroup performance differences, and minimum sample-size or confidence requirements for reliable subgroup estimates.

A prospective governance approach should therefore specify minimum standards for drift detection, reporting cadence, cohort-disaggregated monitoring, and response protocols that activate when clinically meaningful deterioration is detected [ 9 ].
One practical approach is to require accountability-chain documentation as a condition of deployment authorization [ 8 , 15 , 37 ].
Developers should disclose key features of training data provenance, known performance limitations, and relevant subgroup performance where feasible [ 25 , 29 ].

Deployment should therefore require site-specific validation, subgroup-based suspension thresholds, and clearly assigned authority to halt use when safety or equity criteria are breached [ 29 , 31 , 36 ].
Governance should therefore recognize AI oversight competency as a core component of professional preparation, clinical privileging, and continuing education.

Governance should therefore move beyond a simple human-in-the-loop requirement toward clearer standards for autonomy thresholds, escalation rules, and minimum conditions for meaningful human control [ 36 ].

A tiered approach that scales governance intensity to the autonomy, scope, and clinical consequences of the AI system may reduce this risk, although operationalizing such proportionality remains an open challenge.

Governance priorities, therefore, include defined escalation thresholds, plain-language disclosure of AI use, access to human review on request, and exclusion criteria for patient groups requiring additional safeguards [ 16 ].

For high-impact systems, the core requirements include predeployment validation proportionate to clinical risk, subgroup-disaggregated performance evaluation, documentation of intended use and known limitations, and clear assignment of responsibility for monitoring, escalation, and suspension [ 9 , 17 , 29 , 31 , 35 , 37 ].

unlisted_practices: Provide patient-facing disclosure of AI involvement and AI mediation in care.
Define minimum explainability expectations proportional to clinical risk, including user-facing disclosure and documentation of justification for override or reliance in high-impact settings.
Define minimum safeguards for AI-mediated care relationships, including continuity protections for higher-risk or vulnerable patients and review of relational impacts in longitudinal deployments.
Classify AI systems by horizon (H1, H2, H3) and scale minimum governance actions to the horizon classification.
Stress-test governance strategies and regulatory proposals against plausible divergent scenarios.
Move from one-time validation toward life cycle review with explicit thresholds for clinically meaningful performance change and reassessment after material updates.
Regulators should adopt adaptive stewardship capacities, including monitoring population-level performance and international coordination on AI oversight.
Define the conditions under which autonomous or low-human-intervention clinical actions are permissible.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint proposing the FF-CAIG conceptual framework for clinical AI governance and foresight, rather than an empirical study.
